title: Gonorrhoea in Obstetrics & Gynaecology
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection of the genital tract can cause cervicitis, urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease. In low‑resource settings diagnosis relies on clinical signs and simple microscopy, with treatment covering co‑infection.

sections.p: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. In women it most often presents as cervicitis; in men as urethritis. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting the organism on microscopy, culture or nucleic‑acid amplification test (NAAT).
b: Gram‑negative diplococci inside neutrophils on Gram stain
Positive NAAT on urine or endocervical swab (gold standard)
Culture on selective Thayer‑Martin media when NAAT unavailable

sections.p: Clinical severity is staged by the extent of local disease and presence of complications.
b: Uncomplicated cervicitis/urethritis – mucopurulent discharge, mild pain
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) – cervical motion tenderness, adnexal pain
Disseminated gonococcal infection – dermatitis, arthritis, tenosynovitis

sections.p: The infection is transmitted by unprotected vaginal, anal or oral sex. In East Africa co‑infection with Chlamydia trachomatis is common, and HIV, TB or malaria may coexist, influencing presentation and management.
b: Neisseria gonorrhoeae – primary pathogen
Concurrent Chlamydia trachomatis – up to 50 % of cases
Co‑existing HIV – higher bacterial load, atypical symptoms

sections.p: Women usually notice a mucopurulent cervical discharge, dysuria and lower abdominal pain. Men present with a purulent urethral discharge and burning on urination. Systemic signs appear only with disseminated disease.
b: Cervical motion tenderness – key sign of PID
Yellow‑green discharge from cervix or urethra
Fever, arthralgia in disseminated infection

sections.p: Select tests that answer the clinical question; if a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative.

t.b: Does the patient have gonococcal organisms? – Presence of intracellular gram‑negative diplococci confirms infection

t.a: NAAT on urine or cervical swab
t.b: Is gonorrhoea present? – Positive result is definitive; if NAAT unavailable, rely on Gram stain and culture
Is the patient pregnant? – Guides drug choice (ceftriaxone safe, avoid doxycycline)
Is there tubo‑ovarian abscess or severe PID? – Detects fluid collections requiring referral

b: Severe pelvic pain with fever – possible tubo‑ovarian abscess
Joint swelling with skin lesions – disseminated gonococcal infection
Pregnancy with active infection – risk of miscarriage, preterm labour

sections.p: Treat gonorrhoea and always cover chlamydia; add agents for common co‑pathogens in low‑resource settings.
Re‑test and partner management are essential to break transmission cycles.
b: Test of cure with NAAT at 1 week if symptoms persist
Treat all sexual partners within 60 days, regardless of symptoms
Counsel on condom use, limit partners, and HIV testing

sections.p: Conditions that produce similar genital discharge.
b: Chlamydial cervicitis – watery discharge, less purulent
Bacterial vaginosis – thin grey discharge, fishy odor, clue cells on microscopy
Trichomoniasis – frothy yellow‑green discharge, motile trophozoites
Gram stain may be negative in early infection or after antibiotics
NAAT can detect dead organisms – positive result does not always mean active infection
Culture sensitivity drops if specimen not transported in proper media

whenToSeekHelp: High fever with severe abdominal pain

faq.q: Why give azithromycin together with ceftriaxone?
faq.a: Because chlamydia co‑infection is common; azithromycin treats it while ceftriaxone targets gonorrhoea.
Yes, repeated or untreated PID can scar the fallopian tubes, leading to infertility.

faq.q: What if NAAT is not available?
faq.a: Rely on Gram stain and clinical picture; treat empirically with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin.

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness – what is your immediate management? — Give ceftriaxone IM, azithromycin PO, consider metronidazole, arrange pregnancy test and partner treatment.
How does disseminated gonococcal infection differ clinically from simple cervicitis? — Presence of dermatitis, migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis; requires IV ceftriaxone and rheumatology input.
Why is doxycycline avoided in a pregnant patient with gonorrhoea? — It is contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal tooth discoloration and bone growth inhibition.

A patient reports recent antibiotic use and Gram stain is negative; NAAT is unavailable. What do you do? — Treat empirically for gonorrhoea and chlamydia because prior antibiotics can suppress microscopy.
What are the key red‑flag features that mandate referral to a higher‑level centre? — Suspected tubo‑ovarian abscess, septic arthritis, or pregnancy with active infection.
Explain why metronidazole is added to the regimen in many East African settings. — High prevalence of Trichomonas and bacterial vaginosis, which can coexist and worsen symptoms.
How would you counsel a patient on preventing reinfection after treatment? — Use condoms consistently, limit partners, ensure all partners are treated, and retest in 3 months.
What laboratory finding could falsely suggest a negative gonorrhoea result? — Poor specimen transport leading to loss of viability for culture; early infection with low bacterial load on Gram stain.
